lessons.title: The alphabet and reading
lessons.objective: Recognise the letters of the Arabic alphabet and read the short vowels.

content.heading: The Arabic alphabet
content.text: Arabic is written from right to left with 28 letters. The shape of a letter changes according to its position in the word: initial, medial, final or isolated. For example « b » (ب) connects to the following letters.

content.heading: The vowels
content.text: Arabic uses short vowel marks above or below the letters: « fatḥa » (a, َ), « ḍamma » (u, ُ) and « kasra » (i, ِ). The long vowels are letters: ā (ا), ū (و), ī (ي).

content.heading: Reading right to left
content.text: You must get used to reading from right to left. The word « kitāb » (book, كتاب) is read starting with the « k ». Most letters connect like continuous handwriting.

exercises.question: In which direction is Arabic read?
How many letters does the Arabic alphabet have?
What does « كتاب » (kitāb) mean?

lessons.audioScript:
A: Mā hādhā?
B: Hādhā kitāb.
A: Wa mā hādhā?
B: Hādhā qalam.

lessons.title: Greetings
lessons.objective: Greet, introduce yourself and reply to polite formulas in Arabic.

content.heading: The salam
content.text: The universal greeting is « as-salāmu ʿalaykum » (peace be upon you), to which one replies « wa ʿalaykum as-salām ». « Marḥaban » is a simpler hello and « ahlan » a warm welcome.

content.heading: Asking how someone is
content.text: Ask how someone is with « kayfa ḥāluk? » (how are you?). Reply « bi-khayr, shukran » (well, thank you) or « al-ḥamdu li-llāh » (thanks be to God, well).

content.heading: Introducing yourself
content.text: To introduce yourself: « ismī … » (my name is). Ask « mā ismuk? » (what is your name?). « Tasharraftu » means "pleased to meet you".

exercises.question: How do you reply to « as-salāmu ʿalaykum »?
How do you ask "what is your name?"
What does « shukran » mean?

lessons.audioScript:
A: as-salāmu ʿalaykum! Kayfa ḥāluk?
B: wa ʿalaykum as-salām! Anā bi-khayr, shukran. Wa anta?
A: al-ḥamdu li-llāh. Mā ismuk?
B: Ismī Karīm.

lessons.title: Numbers
lessons.objective: Count from 0 to 20 and give your phone number in Arabic.

content.heading: The digits
content.text: The digits used in modern Arabic: ٠ (0), ١ (1), ٢ (2), ٣ (3), ٤ (4), ٥ (5), ٦ (6), ٧ (7), ٨ (8), ٩ (9). In speech: ṣifr, wāḥid, ithnān, thalātha, arbaʿa, khamsa, sitta, sabʿa, thamāniya, tisʿa.

content.heading: Counting from 10 to 20
content.text: From 10 to 20: ʿashara (10), aḥada ʿashar (11), ithnā ʿashar (12), thalāthata ʿashar (13)… up to ʿishrūn (20). In Arabic, the numbers 11 to 19 are built with « ʿashar ».

content.heading: The telephone
content.text: A phone number is read digit by digit. Use the expression « raqam » (number): « raqm al-hātif » is the phone number. In Levantine Arabic, « hātif » means the telephone.

exercises.question: How do you say "five" in Arabic?
How do you say "ten"?
What does « raqm » mean?

lessons.audioScript:
A: Mā raqm al-hātif?
B: Raqmī wāḥid, khamsa, sitta, sitta, sitta.
A: Shukran. Raqmuka wāḥid khamsa sitta sitta sitta.

lessons.title: The family
lessons.objective: Introduce your family and use the possessives in Arabic.

content.heading: The close family
content.text: Close relatives: al-abb (the father), al-umm (the mother), al-akh (the brother), al-ukht (the sister). The plural « al-wālidān » means the parents. « al-ʿāʼila » means the family.

content.heading: The extended family
content.text: Further: al-jadd (the grandfather), al-jadda (the grandmother), al-ʿamm (the paternal uncle), al-khāl (the maternal uncle), al-ʿamma (the paternal aunt), al-khāla (the maternal aunt).

content.heading: Expressing possession
content.text: Arabic adds a possessive suffix to the noun: « abī » (my father), « ummī » (my mother), « akhī » (my brother). For "your", add « -ka » (masculine) or « -ki » (feminine): « abūk » (your father).

exercises.question: How do you say "the mother" in Arabic?
How do you say "my father"?
What does « al-ʿāʼila » mean?

lessons.audioScript:
A: Hal ʿindaka ʿāʼila kabīra?
B: Naʿam, ʿindī ab wa umm wa akhān. Wa anta?
A: ʿindī umm wa ukht waḥida.

lessons.title: Daily life
lessons.objective: Describe your daily activities and use the present-tense verb.

content.heading: The morning
content.text: The day begins with « astayqiẓ » (I wake up) and « atanāwalu al-fuṭūr » (I have breakfast). « Adhhabu ilā al-ʿamal » means I go to work.

content.heading: Present-tense verbs
content.text: In Arabic, the present tense is formed with prefixes: « a- » (I), « ta- » (you), « ya- » (he), « na- » (we). Example: adhhabu (I go), tadhhabu (you go), yadhhabu (he goes).

content.heading: The evening
content.text: In the evening you « arjiʿu ilā al-bayt » (go home) and « atashā ʿashāʼ » (have dinner). « Anāmu » means I sleep. Times: fī al-ṣabāḥ (in the morning), fī al-masāʼ (in the evening).

exercises.question: How do you say "I go to work"?
What does « al-bayt » mean?
How do you say "in the morning"?

lessons.audioScript:
A: Mathā tafʿal fī al-ṣabāḥ?
B: Astayqiẓ fī as-sāʿa as-sādisa, thumma atanāwalu al-fuṭūr.
A: Wa fī al-masāʼ?
B: Arjiʿu ilā al-bayt wa atashā ʿashāʼ.

lessons.title: Food and drink
lessons.objective: Order food, express your tastes and ask politely in Arabic.

content.heading: Foods
content.text: Common foods: khubz (bread), uruzz (rice), laḥm (meat), samak (fish), khudrāwāt (vegetables), fākiha (fruit). Drinks: māʼ (water), shāy (tea), qahwa (coffee), ḥalīb (milk).

content.heading: At the restaurant
content.text: To order: « urīd … » (I want) or « aʿṭinī …, min faḍlik » (give me …, please). The bill: « al-ḥisāb » (the bill). The waiter asks « mādhā tashāʼ? » (what would you like?).

content.heading: Expressing your tastes
content.text: « Uḥibbu » means I like: « uḥibbu al-qahwa » (I like coffee). The negative: « lā uḥibbu al-shāy » (I don't like tea). « Ḥalāl » refers to what is permitted by religion.

exercises.question: How do you say "bread" in Arabic?
How do you ask for the bill?
What does « uḥibbu » mean?

lessons.audioScript:
A: Mādhā tashāʼ?
B: Urīd khubz wa qahwa, min faḍlik.
A: Ahlan wa sahlan. Ayy shayʾ ākhar?
B: Lā, shukran. Al-ḥisāb, min faḍlik.

lessons.title: Housing
lessons.objective: Describe your home and ask for simple directions.

content.heading: Housing
content.text: You live in « bayt » (the house) or « shaqqa » (the flat). The rooms: al-maṭbakh (the kitchen), ghurfat al-nawm (the bedroom), al-ḥammām (the bathroom), ghurfat al-julūs (the living room).

content.heading: Furniture
content.text: Furniture: al-ṭāwila (the table), al-kursī (the chair), al-sarīr (the bed), al-khizāna (the cupboard). « Fī al-bayt » means in the house.

content.heading: Finding your way
content.text: To find your way: « ayna …? » (where is …?), « ilā al-yamīn » (to the right), « ilā al-yasār » (to the left), « mustaqīman » (straight on). Example: « Ayna al-bank? » (where is the bank?).

exercises.question: How do you say "the house" in Arabic?
How do you ask "where is the bank?"
What does « ilā al-yamīn » mean?

lessons.audioScript:
A: Ayna al-bank, min faḍlik?
B: Al-bank hunāk, ilā al-yamīn.
A: Ilā al-yamīn. Shukran jazeelan!
B: ʿAfwan.

lessons.title: Time and the days
lessons.objective: Give the time and the days of the week, and make an appointment.

content.heading: The time
content.text: Ask the time with « kam as-sāʿa? » (what time is it?). Reply « as-sāʿa thalātha » (it is three o'clock). « Al-niṣf » means half past: as-sāʿa thalātha wa-n-niṣf (half past three).

content.heading: The days of the week
content.text: The days: al-ithnayn (Monday), ath-thulāthāʼ (Tuesday), al-arbiʿāʼ (Wednesday), al-khamīs (Thursday), al-jumʿa (Friday), as-sabt (Saturday), al-aḥad (Sunday). Friday, the holy day, is often a holiday.

content.heading: Making an appointment
content.text: « Mawʿid » means the appointment. Suggest: « hal nataqābal yawm al-ithnayn? » (shall we meet on Monday?). « Fī al-thalātha » specifies "at three o'clock".

exercises.question: How do you ask the time?
What does « as-sāʿa thalātha wa-n-niṣf » mean?
Which day is « al-jumʿa »?

lessons.audioScript:
A: Kam as-sāʿa?
B: As-sāʿa al-khāmisa wa-n-niṣf.
A: Hal nataqābal ghadan?
B: Naʿam, ghadan fī as-sāʿa as-sādisa.

lessons.title: Shopping
lessons.objective: Ask a price, buy and bargain simply at the market.

content.heading: At the market
content.text: At the market (as-sūq), the seller says « Ahlan wa sahlan » (welcome). Ask the price: « kam al-thaman? » (how much does it cost?). Trade often involves some bargaining.

content.heading: Asking a price
content.text: « Bikam hādhā? » (how much is this?). The answer: « bi-ʿashara dīnār » (ten dinars). « Ghālī » means expensive, « rakhīṣ » cheap. You can say « hādhā ghālī jiddan » (this is very expensive).

content.heading: Buying and paying
content.text: To buy: « sa-ākhudh hādhā » (I will take this). « Anāqid » means I pay. In cash: naqdan. The question « hal taqbalu al-bāqāt? » asks whether card payment is accepted.

exercises.question: How do you ask the price?
What does « ghālī » mean?
How do you say "I will take this"?

lessons.audioScript:
A: Bikam hādhā al-qamīṣ?
B: Hādhā al-qamīṣ bi-ʿishrīn dīnār.
A: Hādhā ghālī jiddan! A-rākhīṣ akhī?
B: Ḥasanan, bikhamsata ʿashar dīnār.

lessons.title: Travel and transport
lessons.objective: Take transport, buy a ticket and move around while travelling.

content.heading: Transport
content.text: Transport: as-sayyāra (the car), al-ḥāfila (the bus), al-qiṭār (the train), aṭ-ṭāʼira (the plane), al-tāksī (the taxi). « Khuḏ al-ḥāfila » means take the bus.

content.heading: Buying a ticket
content.text: At the counter: « uḥtāju tadhkara ilā … » (I need a ticket to …). « Dhahāb » means single, « dhahāb wa-iyāb » return. « Matā yughādir al-qiṭār? » (when does the train leave?).

content.heading: At the airport and the station
content.text: The platform is « ar-riṣīf », the departure « al-inṭilāq » and the arrival « al-wuṣūl ». « Mataḥṭa » means the station. Ask the route with « kayfa adhhabu ilā …? » (how do I get to …?).

exercises.question: How do you say "the train" in Arabic?
How do you say "return trip"?
What does « al-maṭār » mean?

lessons.audioScript:
A: Uḥtāju tadhkara ilā al-Qāhira, min faḍlik.
B: Dhahāb am dhahāb wa-iyāb?
A: Dhahāb. Matā yughādir al-qiṭār?
B: Fī as-sāʿa al-ʿāshira.
